results.caption_gt: Histopathology of Paget disease (hematoxylin and eosin stain). The image shows nests of pale-staining tumor cells, also known as Paget’s cells, arranged singly or in small clusters along the vulvar epidermis. These tumor cells typically have abundant pale cytoplasm and large nuclei with a prominent, vesicular nucleus, and may display unusual mitotic figures. The tumor commonly locates in the epidermis, with occasional dermal invasion. This histopathological diagnosis is crucial as this entity can be confused with other neoplasms such as melanoma, Bowen’s disease, or sebaceous carcinoma.

The image shows nests of pigmented nevus cells that are clearly separated from the epithelial lining by an evident basement membrane. The subepithelial region contains polygonal and epithelioid cells, while deeper cells resemble lymphocytes. Oral melanocytic nevi are rare benign neoplasms, often found on the palate, and are diagnosed on average in the third and fourth decades of life. Histologically, intramucosal nevi frequently exhibit cells arranged in nests, with polygonal and epithelioid cell types observed. Small, dense nuclei resembling lymphocytes (Type B nevus cells) are also characteristic, and melanin pigment is commonly present within the cytoplasm.

While intramucosal nevi commonly show polygonal and epithelioid cells, the presence of spindle-shaped cells with neurotization (Type C cells) is also a recognized feature, observed in some cases in this study and associated with the maturation process. results.caption_gt: Histopathology by H&E stain showing involvement of the dermis predominantly by spindle-shaped Schwannian cells and small nests of round melanocytes at 40X magnification. The histopathological examination revealed extensive involvement of the dermis by small nests of spindle-shaped melanocytes. Increased vascularity was noted, along with clusters of small, round melanocytes interspersed between collagen bundles and around epithelial adnexal structures, extending into the subcutaneous septa and between adipocytes. Rare pagetoid arrays of melanocytes were also observed as both single cells and round nests, with pale, vacuolated cytoplasm and dusty melanin. No alarming features, such as increased mitotic activity or perineural invasion, were identified. These findings were interpreted as NCH (Nodular Cellular Nevus) with Schwannian differentiation and focal mild atypical features within a CMN (Congenital Melanocytic Nevus), highlighting the complexity of this lesion.

results.caption_gt: Histopathological image of tumoral melanosis (TM) at ×10 magnification, stained with hematoxylin and eosin. The image is characterized by mild stromal reorganization with fibrosis, lymphoid inflammation with rare plasma cells, and massive accumulation of melanophages. From a histological point of view, TM is considered a complete regression of melanoma, characterized by the complete absence of dermal or junctional melanocytes, with the lesion area entirely replaced by varying degrees of fibrosis, inflammation, and sometimes abundant melanophages in the site of a previously documented pigmented lesion.

results.caption_gt: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained image of a representative tissue section of melanoma brain metastasis from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill craniotomy cohort. results.caption_gt: Photomicrograph showing a prototypical Spitz nevus, a benign melanocytic proliferation. This low-magnification view (original magnification 10×) highlights the distinctive architectural features of the lesion, which is symmetric, slightly raised, and compound, demonstrating a maturating melanocytic proliferation with epidermal hyperplasia and a flat base. The lesion often presents with a dome-shaped, wedge-shaped, or plaque-like silhouette, characterized by sharp lateral borders and maturation towards the deep part. Scattered Kamino bodies, which are small to large dull eosinophilic globules composed of amorphous filaments, may be seen. The pattern of growth is predominantly nested, composed of spindle and epithelioid melanocytes. The image is stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E).

results.caption_gt: Photomicrograph illustrating a prototypical Spitz nevus, a benign melanocytic proliferation. This view (original magnification 100×) shows the characteristic architectural and cytological features, including large clefting nests of spindle and epithelioid melanocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The lesion exhibits epidermal hyperplasia, and the overlying epidermis may be separated from the junctional nests and single melanocytes by clefts. Nests often display varying cellularity, size, and shape, and are typically arranged in parallel to the rete ridges. Scattered Kamino bodies, which are dull eosinophilic globules composed of amorphous filaments, are also present. The melanocytes feature moderately pleomorphic vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. There is a predominance of enlarged epithelioid and/or spindle melanocytes with abundant eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm, often with a “ground-glass” appearance, and round to oval to spindle nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin and distinct nucleoli. The image is stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E).

results.caption_gt: Histopathology showing architectural features of a sinonasal mucosal melanoma, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The tumor is observed growing as a polypoid, edematous, and highly vascularized mass, with melanoma involving the entire polyp as multiple confluent nodules, reaching at least 1 mm Breslow thickness. The transitional respiratory epithelium is still recognizable all around. Mucosal melanomas are often characterized by significant cytological variability, including spindle, rhabdoid, epithelioid, small, or giant pleomorphic (often multinucleated) cells, which can pose diagnostic challenges in differentiating them from lymphomas, carcinomas, or sarcomas. Necrotic areas are frequently observed, and mitotic activity is typically high. While many mucosal melanomas are associated with an in situ lateral spread on the mucosal surface, their heterogeneous presentation often necessitates immunohistochemical staining (e.g., S100, MART-1, HMB45, or SOX10) to confirm their melanocytic origin.
